title: Accounting Standard 28 Impairment of Assets
outcomes: Measure recoverable amount using net selling price and value in use.
Recognise and allocate impairment losses for assets and CGUs.
Account for reversals and give disclosures.

meta.exam_tip: Recoverable amount is the higher of the two measures; allocate CGU losses to goodwill first and respect the floors.

concepts.title: When to test: indications of impairment
body: An asset is impaired when its carrying amount is more than its recoverable amount. At each balance sheet date the enterprise checks for any indication of impairment; only if there is one does it estimate recoverable amount.

External signs: a sharp fall in market value beyond normal use; adverse changes in technology, market, economy or law; rise in market interest rates that raises discount rates; net assets carried above market capitalisation.
Internal signs: obsolescence or physical damage; plans to discontinue, restructure or dispose of the asset; internal reports showing worse economic performance than expected.
AS 28 covers most assets, but not inventories, construction contract assets, deferred tax assets, financial assets within AS 13 and assets arising from employee benefits.
concepts.analogy: Look for warning signs every year; measure only when a sign appears.
concepts.work: A new law banning diesel generators in the city signals impairment of a company's diesel gensets.

concepts.title: Recoverable amount: net selling price and value in use
body: Recoverable amount = whichever is greater: net selling price or value in use.
Net selling price: the amount obtainable from selling the asset in an arm's length transaction, less costs of disposal (excluding finance costs and tax).

Value in use: present value of estimated future cash flows from continuing use and disposal at the end of its life. Cash flows are pre-tax, based on reasonable and supportable assumptions, use budgets for up to five years normally, exclude financing and tax flows, and exclude future restructuring or improvements not yet committed. The discount rate is a pre-tax rate reflecting time value and asset-specific risks.
If either measure exceeds the carrying amount, no impairment exists and the other need not be computed.
concepts.analogy: An asset is worth the better of selling it now or using it on.
concepts.work: If an old truck can be sold for more than its book value, no value-in-use calculation is needed.

concepts.title: Recognising an impairment loss
body: Impairment loss = carrying amount − recoverable amount. It is recognised as an expense in profit and loss, unless the asset is carried at a revalued amount, in which case it is first set off against the revaluation surplus for that asset.
After recognition, depreciation in future periods is based on the revised carrying amount over the remaining useful life.
If the loss exceeds the carrying amount, a liability is recognised only if another standard requires it.
concepts.analogy: Write the asset down to what it can recover, and depreciate from there.
concepts.work: A revalued building with ₹5 lakh surplus suffering a ₹7 lakh impairment: ₹5 lakh against surplus, ₹2 lakh to profit and loss.

concepts.title: Cash-generating units, goodwill and corporate assets
body: If recoverable amount cannot be estimated for an individual asset, it is estimated for the cash-generating unit (CGU) to which it belongs — the smallest identifiable group of assets producing cash inflows largely independent of other assets.

Goodwill: a bottom-up test checks whether goodwill can be allocated reasonably to the CGU; if not, a top-down test applies to the smallest larger unit to which goodwill can be allocated. Corporate assets (head office, IT centre) are handled the same way.

A CGU's impairment loss is allocated first to goodwill, then to other assets pro rata on carrying amounts. No asset is reduced below the highest of its net selling price, value in use (if determinable) and zero; any shortfall is spread over the other assets.
concepts.analogy: When assets earn only together, test them together.
concepts.work: A bus route's buses, depot and permits form one CGU if the route's cash flows are independent.

concepts.title: Reversal of impairment loss and disclosure
body: At each balance sheet date the enterprise checks whether an earlier impairment loss may no longer exist or may have decreased; if so, recoverable amount is re-estimated.

A reversal increases the carrying amount, but not above what it would have been (net of depreciation) had no impairment been recognised. It is credited to profit and loss, unless the asset is revalued, when it goes to revaluation surplus (after reversing any loss earlier charged to profit and loss).
An impairment loss on goodwill is reversed only if the loss came from an unusual one-off outside event not expected to recur, and later external events have reversed its effect.

Disclose impairment losses and reversals by class and line item, losses against revaluation surplus, and for material losses the events, amount, nature of asset or CGU, segment, and whether recoverable amount is net selling price or value in use (with discount rate).
concepts.analogy: Reversals are allowed, but never above the "no-impairment" carrying amount.
concepts.work: An asset written down to ₹40 lakh, which would now be ₹45 lakh without impairment, cannot be restored above ₹45 lakh.

illustrations.title: Testing one machine
illustrations.q: A machine of Varsha Ltd. has a carrying amount of ₹50 lakh. Demand for its output has fallen. It could be sold for ₹40 lakh with disposal costs of ₹2 lakh. If kept, it will generate net cash inflows of ₹15 lakh a year for 3 years; discount rate 10% (factors 0.9091, 0.8264, 0.7513). Compute the impairment loss.

solution.text: The loss is charged to profit and loss (the machine is carried at cost). Future depreciation is based on the new carrying amount of ₹38 lakh.

illustrations.title: Allocating a unit's loss
illustrations.q: A cash-generating unit of Ojas Ltd. carries goodwill ₹10 lakh, machinery ₹60 lakh and building ₹40 lakh. Its recoverable amount is ₹80 lakh. No individual asset's recoverable amount is determinable. Allocate the impairment loss.

solution.text: After goodwill, the loss is spread over other assets in proportion to carrying amounts — but no asset goes below the highest of its net selling price, value in use (if determinable) and zero.

Impairment loss of the unit (₹ lakh)

jobs.title: Year-end impairment review
jobs.situation: A plant's output prices have fallen 25% and the company's market capitalisation is below book value.
steps: Estimate net selling price and value in use.
Allocate any loss and update depreciation.
jobs.takeaway: Indicators trigger the test; recoverable amount decides the loss.

options: The higher of net selling price and value in use
The lower of net selling price and value in use
mcqs.explain: Under AS 28, recoverable amount is whichever is greater — what the asset would sell for net of costs, or its value in use — because a rational owner would choose the better of selling or using. In practice: compute the easier one first.
mcqs.topic: Recoverable amount: net selling price and value in use

mcqs.q: Which is an external indication of impairment?
options: Carrying amount of net assets exceeds market capitalisation
A plan to restructure the division
mcqs.explain: Net assets above market capitalisation is an external sign; damage, restructuring plans and poor internal performance are internal signs. Both kinds trigger an estimate of recoverable amount. In practice: list signs every year end.
mcqs.topic: When to test: indications of impairment

mcqs.q: Cash flows used for value in use should:
options: Exclude financing and income tax flows
Include planned future improvements not yet committed
mcqs.explain: Value in use uses pre-tax operating cash flows from the asset in its current condition, discounted at a pre-tax rate. Financing, tax and uncommitted improvements or restructurings are excluded. In practice: avoid double counting interest.
mcqs.topic: Recoverable amount: net selling price and value in use

mcqs.q: Carrying amount ₹30 lakh; net selling price ₹24 lakh; value in use ₹27 lakh. Impairment loss:
mcqs.explain: Recoverable amount is the higher of ₹24 lakh and ₹27 lakh, i.e. ₹27 lakh. Loss = ₹30 − 27 = ₹3 lakh, charged to profit and loss for an asset carried at cost. In practice: depreciate ₹27 lakh hereafter.

mcqs.q: An impairment loss on a revalued asset is:
options: First set off against its revaluation surplus
Always charged to profit and loss
mcqs.explain: For an asset carried at revalued amount, the impairment loss is treated as a revaluation decrease — first against the surplus for that asset, with any excess in profit and loss. In practice: track surplus asset by asset.

options: The smallest identifiable group of assets generating largely independent cash inflows
mcqs.explain: A CGU is the smallest identifiable group of assets whose continuing use produces cash inflows largely independent of those from other assets or groups. It is used when individual recoverable amounts cannot be estimated. In practice: look at independent revenue streams.
mcqs.topic: Cash-generating units, goodwill and corporate assets

mcqs.q: An impairment loss of a CGU is allocated first to:
mcqs.explain: AS 28 allocates the loss first to reduce goodwill of the unit, and then to other assets pro rata on carrying amounts, subject to floors. In practice: goodwill usually absorbs the first hit.
mcqs.topic: Cash-generating units, goodwill and corporate assets

mcqs.q: A reversal of impairment can increase the carrying amount up to:
options: What it would have been, net of depreciation, without the impairment
mcqs.explain: A reversal is capped at the carrying amount that would have existed, after depreciation, had no impairment loss been recognised earlier. Anything more would be a revaluation. In practice: keep a shadow depreciation schedule.
mcqs.topic: Reversal of impairment loss and disclosure

mcqs.q: An impairment loss on goodwill can be reversed only if:
options: It was caused by an exceptional external event not expected to recur and later events reversed it
mcqs.explain: Goodwill impairment reversals are allowed only where the loss arose from an unusual one-off outside event that is not likely to happen again, and later external events have reversed its effect. In practice: such reversals are rare.
mcqs.topic: Reversal of impairment loss and disclosure

mcqs.q: Is an annual estimate of recoverable amount required for every asset?
options: No; only when there is an indication of impairment (with specified exceptions)
mcqs.explain: AS 28 requires an assessment of indications at each balance sheet date; recoverable amount is estimated only when an indication exists, except where other standards require annual testing, such as long-lived intangibles. In practice: document the assessment.
mcqs.topic: When to test: indications of impairment

questions.q: A machine of Varsha Ltd. has a carrying amount of ₹50 lakh. Demand for its output has fallen. It could be sold for ₹40 lakh with disposal costs of ₹2 lakh. If kept, it will generate net cash inflows of ₹15 lakh a year for 3 years; discount rate 10% (factors 0.9091, 0.8264, 0.7513). Compute the impairment loss.

model.text: The loss is charged to profit and loss (the machine is carried at cost). Future depreciation is based on the new carrying amount of ₹38 lakh.

mistakes: Taking the lower of the two.

questions.q: A cash-generating unit of Ojas Ltd. carries goodwill ₹10 lakh, machinery ₹60 lakh and building ₹40 lakh. Its recoverable amount is ₹80 lakh. No individual asset's recoverable amount is determinable. Allocate the impairment loss.

model.text: After goodwill, the loss is spread over other assets in proportion to carrying amounts — but no asset goes below the highest of its net selling price, value in use (if determinable) and zero.

mistakes: Spreading the loss over goodwill and assets together.

Impairment loss of the unit (₹ lakh)

summary: Check indications every balance sheet date.
Recoverable = higher of NSP and value in use.
Loss = carrying − recoverable; P&L or revaluation surplus.
CGU: smallest independent cash-generating group; goodwill bottom-up/top-down.
Allocate: goodwill first, then pro rata with floors.
Reversal capped at no-impairment carrying amount; goodwill rarely.
remember: Value in use uses pre-tax flows and rate.
traps: Recoverable amount is the higher, not the lower.

viva.model: When its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount.
The present value of estimated future cash flows while the asset keeps being used, plus what its final sale should bring.

viva.q: How is a CGU's impairment loss allocated?
viva.model: First to goodwill of the unit, then to other assets pro rata to carrying amounts, without taking any asset below the highest of net selling price, value in use and zero.

viva.q: What is the limit on reversing an impairment loss?
viva.model: The increased carrying amount cannot exceed what it would have been, net of depreciation, had no impairment been recognised.

viva.q: Give two internal indications of impairment.
viva.model: Obsolescence or physical damage, plans to discontinue or restructure, and internal reports showing worse economic performance.

cases.title: Rohini Textiles Ltd.
cases.case: Rohini Textiles Ltd. has a weaving unit (a CGU) carrying goodwill ₹5 crore, looms ₹30 crore and shed ₹15 crore. Cheap imports have cut demand. Recoverable amount of the unit is ₹38 crore. The shed alone can be sold for ₹14 crore net.

mcqs.explain: Carrying amount of the unit is ₹5 + 30 + 15 = ₹50 crore; recoverable amount ₹38 crore; loss ₹12 crore. In practice: confirm the CGU boundaries first.
mcqs.topic: Cash-generating units, goodwill and corporate assets

mcqs.q: Loss allocated to the shed (before applying its floor):
mcqs.explain: After writing off goodwill of ₹5 crore, ₹7 crore remains, split 30:15 between looms and shed: shed ₹2.33 crore. In practice: then apply the floor.
mcqs.topic: Cash-generating units, goodwill and corporate assets

mcqs.q: The shed's floor of ₹14 crore means its loss is limited to:
options: ₹1 crore, with the rest moved to the looms
mcqs.explain: The shed cannot go below its net selling price of ₹14 crore, so it can absorb only ₹1 crore; the remaining ₹1.33 crore is reallocated to the looms. In practice: re-run the allocation.
mcqs.topic: Cash-generating units, goodwill and corporate assets
